CVTSplat: Multi-view Reconstruction Using an Adaptive Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation

CCS: Computing methodologies ReconstructionCCS: Computing methodologies Shape representations
Briac Toussaint Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarbrücken, Germany email: btoussai@mpi-inf.mpg.de , Diego Thomas Affiliation: Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan email: thomas@ait.kyushu-u.ac.jp , Jean-Sébastien Franco Affiliation: Inria, Grenoble, France email: jean-sebastien.franco@inria.fr , Edmond Boyer Affiliation: Inria, Grenoble, France email: edmond.boyer@inria.fr and Christian Theobalt Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Informatics, Saarbrücken, Germany email: theobalt@mpi-inf.mpg.de
Abstract.

Voronoi tessellations have recently emerged as an adaptive, space-partitioning discretization for shape and appearance reconstruction from multi-view images. However, the irregular cells they produce make the repeated reconstruction of the tessellation during optimization costly. We therefore explore adaptive centroidal Voronoi tessellations (CVTs), which extend standard CVTs with non-uniform cell sizes while preserving the regular, well-shaped cells that make them efficient to compute. In CVTSplat, cell size is modulated by the evolving signed distance field, concentrating sites near the zero level set while keeping cells nearly centroidal. This regularity lets us specialize the whole pipeline, with GPU algorithms for nearest-neighbor queries and approximate Voronoi construction, and a rasterizer tailored to small, nearly isotropic cells. Our Voronoi construction is 5–10× faster than general-purpose alternatives in this regime. On DTU and BlendedMVS, CVTSplat reaches geometric accuracy competitive with the best Gaussian-splatting surface methods while training in about 2.5 minutes on a single GPU.

Keywords: 
Multiview Reconstruction, Voronoi Diagram, Implicit Surface

1. Introduction

Multi-view reconstruction aims at recovering the geometry and appearance of a 3D scene from a collection of images acquired from different viewpoints. A central challenge is to design a representation that provides sufficient spatial resolution to capture fine surface details while remaining computationally efficient to optimize and render. Implicit surface methods coupled with differentiable rendering have demonstrated high reconstruction quality (Wang et al., 2021), but their practical efficiency and compactness strongly depend on how the scene volume is discretized. Uniform discretizations, such as dense voxel grids, allocate the same capacity throughout space even though accurate geometry and appearance are primarily required near the reconstructed surface. Conversely, adaptive representations concentrate capacity in relevant regions, but introduce irregular spatial configurations that can make neighborhood queries, geometric operations, and rendering more expensive.

Voronoi-based representations provide an interesting direction for addressing this trade-off. Recent works have explored Voronoi and related cellular discretizations for neural rendering and reconstruction (Govindarajan et al., 2025; Govindarajan et al., 2026; Rech et al., 2026; Mai et al., 2026; Taveira et al., 2026b; Weidenfeller et al., 2026). However, these representations do not explicitly exploit one of the fundamental properties of Centroidal Voronoi Tessellations (CVTs): their tendency to produce regular, well-shaped cells. Such regularity is particularly attractive computationally, since irregular Voronoi cells may require visiting many neighboring sites when constructing the diagram (Ray et al., 2018). At the same time, a standard CVT tends toward a uniform distribution of sites, thereby losing the main benefit of an adaptive representation.

We therefore investigate adaptive centroidal Voronoi tessellations as a spatial representation for multi-view reconstruction. We modulate cell size using the implicit surface, yielding a near-centroidal tessellation with increased site density around the zero level set (fig. 1). This combines the representational efficiency of an adaptive discretization with the computational benefits of regular Voronoi cells, while relying on a standard Voronoi diagram rather than a power diagram. Specifically, power diagrams offer another way to achieve adaptivity, but require an additional weight per site and incur a higher construction cost (Govindarajan et al., 2026; Taveira et al., 2026a).

Based on this representation, we introduce CVTSplat, a differentiable multi-view reconstruction method in which each Voronoi site carries a signed-distance value and compact appearance attributes decoded into view-dependent radiance. The near-centroidal structure of the tessellation lets us specialize every stage of the pipeline to this regime. Since well-shaped cells have few and nearby neighbors, the Voronoi diagram can be constructed from a small set of candidate sites. We deliberately accept an approximate diagram in the rare cases where this set is incomplete, as the resulting local overlaps are compatible with differentiable primitive-based rendering (Kerbl et al., 2023). Similarly, instead of ray tracing an exact diagram (Govindarajan et al., 2025), we directly rasterize the cells (Govindarajan et al., 2026) and exploit their small, nearly isotropic shape to tailor the rasterizer. Together, these choices make CVTSplat a regular yet surface-adaptive discretization for efficient geometry and appearance reconstruction.

The complete optimization pipeline is described in figure 2. It consists of two components: the adaptive tessellation controls the position of the sites, while the differentiable rendering branch optimizes the signed-distance and appearance attributes. The tessellation is guided by the evolving implicit surface to produce a surface-adaptive discretization. Our main contributions are as follows:

  1. (1)

    We introduce an adaptive centroidal Voronoi discretization for multi-view reconstruction, combining surface adaptivity with the regularity of centroidal tessellations. Our complete reconstruction pipeline achieves geometric accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art 3DGS-based methods (Chen et al., 2024; Gomez et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b) on DTU, while training in approximately 2.5 minutes on a single RTX 5090 and using 4 GB of VRAM.

  2. (2)

    We exploit the regularity of the tessellation to make Voronoi-based reconstruction computationally efficient. We introduce specialized GPU algorithms for approximate Voronoi construction, repeated KK-nearest-neighbor queries, and Delaunay triangulation, substantially accelerating these operations compared to general-purpose approaches (Ray et al., 2018; Basselin et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2014; Taveira et al., 2026a; Govindarajan et al., 2025).

  3. (3)

    We propose a rasterizer optimized for rendering small, isotropic primitives, further consolidating our framework.

2. Related Work

We review the literature most closely related to our approach along three directions: adaptive spatial discretizations for implicit 3D reconstruction (Sec. 2.1), explicit primitive-based representations (Sec. 2.2), and efficient GPU construction of 3D Voronoi and Delaunay diagrams (Sec. 2.3).

2.1. Adaptive Spatial Discretizations

Multi-view 3D reconstruction based on differentiable rendering initially relied on continuous neural representations (Mildenhall et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021), before increasingly adopting grid-based or hybrid spatial encodings to accelerate optimization and rendering (Fridovich-Keil et al., 2022; Müller et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020; Toussaint et al., 2025). The main objective of these representations is to allocate computation sparsely, by concentrating capacity around the reconstructed surface. However, grid-aligned discretizations typically follow a predefined spatial structure that either stays fixed during optimization or changes discretely across levels of detail.

Unstructured discretizations offer greater flexibility in adapting both the number and spatial extent of their elements. Recent approaches have explored Voronoi or Power cells (Govindarajan et al., 2025; Govindarajan et al., 2026; Rech et al., 2026; Taveira et al., 2026b), as well as tetrahedral representations (Thomas et al., 2025; Kulhanek and Sattler, 2023; Mai et al., 2026; Weidenfeller et al., 2026). These works motivate spatial representations that retain the flexibility of unstructured discretizations while achieving the accuracy and efficiency of highly optimized grid-based methods.

2.2. Explicit Splatting Representations

3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) has become a widely used representation for high-quality novel-view synthesis due to its adaptive distribution of primitives and efficient rasterization. However, recovering coherent geometry from an unstructured set of Gaussians is highly challenging (Guédon and Lepetit, 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024; Radl et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024; Guédon et al., 2025; Gomez et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Existing methods introduce additional constraints or regularization to suppress floaters and improve depth and normal consistency (Chen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b), or dedicated procedures for extracting closed surfaces (Guédon et al., 2025; Gomez et al., 2026).

Space-partitioning primitives such as tetrahedra and Voronoi cells provide an alternative splat support (Govindarajan et al., 2025; Mai et al., 2026) in which neighboring elements form a coherent spatial decomposition rather than an overlapping collection of primitives. This structure provides consistent spatial ordering, but maintaining it while the underlying sites move during optimization can introduce considerable computational overhead. Efficiently updating such adaptive representations therefore remains an important challenge.

2.3. GPU Voronoi & Delaunay Diagrams Construction

A 3D Voronoi diagram can be represented through its adjacency graph, i.e., the neighboring relationships between generating sites. This graph can be recovered indirectly through the dual Delaunay triangulation (Govindarajan et al., 2025), or computed directly from the Voronoi cells. GPU Delaunay algorithms enable substantial parallelism (Cao et al., 2014; Govindarajan et al., 2025), but generally require multiple rounds of point insertion, tetrahedron splitting, flipping, and repair, making frequent reconstruction of a dynamically evolving diagram costly.

GPU methods for direct Voronoi construction were initially developed for relatively uniform point distributions (Ray et al., 2018; Basselin et al., 2021), providing large speedups over CPU implementations (The CGAL Project, 2026; Lévy, 2026). More recently, Taveira et al. (Taveira et al., 2026a) extended this family of approaches to non-uniform point distributions. Following the clipping formulation of Ray et al. (Ray et al., 2018), Voronoi cells are constructed independently by successively clipping them against bisector planes induced by neighboring sites. Although cells can be processed in parallel, the clipping operations for each cell are sequential, and irregular cells may require significantly more operations. Leaving cells unregularized (Govindarajan et al., 2025) can thereby increase the total construction cost.

3. Fast and Adaptive Spatial Data Structure

Our spatial representation consists of a set of sites {𝐱i}0≤i<N\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{0\leq i<N} (i.e. 3D points) that induce a Voronoi tessellation of the scene volume. Each site stores the geometric and appearance attributes used by the reconstruction, including a signed-distance value and view-dependent radiance features. The Voronoi cells provide the volumetric primitives used for rendering, while their dual Delaunay connectivity provides the local neighborhood structure required for mesh extraction. Because the site positions evolve throughout optimization, these structures must be updated repeatedly. A key property of our representation is that the sites remain close to a centroidal configuration, producing compact cells with a small number of nearby neighbors and enabling efficient GPU construction.

In the following, we first describe how we obtain this adaptive centroidal distribution (Sec. 3.1) and compute its centroids (Sec. 3.2). We then present our fast Voronoi construction (Sec. 3.3), its conversion to Delaunay tetrahedra (Sec. 3.4), and the KNN kernel supporting these operations (Sec. 3.5).

3.1. Adaptive Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation

In a centroidal Voronoi tessellation (CVT), the sites 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} coincide with the center of mass 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i} of their cell (the centroids). It is not the case at first because the sites have arbitrary positions, but iteratively minimizing the CVT loss ℒCVT=∑‖𝐱i−𝐱¯i‖2\mathcal{L}_{\text{CVT}}=\sum||\mathbf{x}_{i}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}||^{2} brings the tessellation closer to being centroidal, with regular cells (Lloyd, 1982). Since we need an adaptive distribution rather than a uniform one, we propose to bias this loss using the normal vector of the SDF (see figure 3). Our biased CVT loss is as follows:

(1) ℒCVT\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{CVT}} =∑i1sg⁡(ri)​‖𝐱i−sg⁡(𝐱¯i−βi​ri​𝐧i)‖22.\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sg}\!\left(r_{i}\right)}||\mathbf{x}_{i}-\operatorname{sg}\!\left(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\beta_{i}r_{i}\mathbf{n}_{i}\right)||_{2}^{2}.

sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}\!\left(\cdot\right) is the stop-gradient operator and rir_{i} is the radius of the cell. Adaptivity may also be achieved using a spatially-varying mass density when computing cell moments (Du et al., 1999) but our approach is more direct. Intuitively, the centroid 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i} is offset by a fraction βi\beta_{i} of the cell radius along the SDF gradient 𝐧i\mathbf{n}_{i}. We divide by rir_{i} to make the loss scale-invariant. βi\beta_{i} directly depends on the SDF f^i\hat{f}_{i}:

(2) βi\displaystyle\beta_{i} =a⋅tanh⁡(f^i2​b).\displaystyle=a\cdot\tanh(\frac{\hat{f}_{i}}{2b}).

a,b>0a,b>0 control the magnitude of the shift. Using a=0a=0 gives the standard centroidal tessellation. In our experiments, we set a=0.1a=0.1 and b=0.001b=0.001 which corresponds to shifting the centroid by 10%10\% of the cell radius. This results in smaller cells near the zero level-set and larger cells further away, with cell radius growing approximately linearly with SDF (refer to the supplementary material for an empirical analysis). The size of the cells is not explicitly imposed, which lets them arrange themselves independently of their number and of the object’s surface area.

3.2. Computation of the Centroids

The CVT loss depends on the centroid 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}, itself depending on the volume 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i}. They can be computed using a tetrahedral decomposition of the cell (Ray et al., 2018) or its polyhedron representation (Mirtich, 1996). We propose a simpler alternative, although approximate, based on Riemann sums. Evaluating these sums only requires knowledge of the bisector planes, directly available from the Voronoi adjacency graph. Specifically, we sample n=64n=64 rays 𝐫k∈S2\mathbf{r}_{k}\in S^{2} from a Fibonacci sphere lattice, and measure the distance lkl_{k} from the site 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} to the nearest bisector plane along 𝐫k\mathbf{r}_{k} (see figure 3, left).

(3) 𝒱i=∫𝒞i𝑑𝐱=∫S2∫0l⁡(𝐫)s2​𝑑s​𝑑σ=∫S2l​(𝐫)33​𝑑σ≈4​π3​n​∑k=0n−1lk3.\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{i}=\int_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}d\mathbf{x}=\int_{S^{2}}\int_{0}^{l(\mathbf{r})}s^{2}dsd\sigma=\int_{S^{2}}\frac{l(\mathbf{r})^{3}}{3}d\sigma\approx\frac{4\pi}{3n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}l_{k}^{3}.

The volume integral over cell 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} is decomposed into a 1D integral and an integral over the unit sphere S2S^{2}. l⁡(𝐫)l(\mathbf{r}) is the distance from the site to the nearest clipping plane along 𝐫\mathbf{r} and d​σd\sigma is an infinitesimal surface element on S2S^{2}. Because the rays are approximately uniformly spread, their weight in the Riemann sum is 4​πn\frac{4\pi}{n}. A similar computation gives the centroid 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}:

(4) 𝐱¯i−𝐱i\displaystyle\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{i} =1𝒱i​∫𝒞i𝐱−𝐱i​𝑑𝐱=1𝒱i​∫S2∫0l⁡(𝐫)𝐫​s⋅s2​𝑑s​𝑑σ\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\mathcal{V}_{i}}\int_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{i}d\mathbf{x}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{V}_{i}}\int_{S^{2}}\int_{0}^{l(\mathbf{r})}\mathbf{r}s\cdot s^{2}dsd\sigma
(5) =1𝒱i​∫S2𝐫​l​(𝐫)44​𝑑σ≈1𝒱i​4​πn​∑k=0n−1𝐫k​lk44=34​∑𝐫k​lk4∑lk3.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\mathcal{V}_{i}}\int_{S^{2}}\mathbf{r}\frac{l(\mathbf{r})^{4}}{4}d\sigma\approx\frac{1}{\mathcal{V}_{i}}\frac{4\pi}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{r}_{k}\frac{l_{k}^{4}}{4}=\frac{3}{4}\frac{\sum\mathbf{r}_{k}l_{k}^{4}}{\sum l_{k}^{3}}.

𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i} and 𝐱¯i\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{i} are re-evaluated at every training iteration. The accuracy of these quadrature formulas is assessed in the appendix. Our approach does not preclude using a more direct computation (Ray et al., 2018; Mirtich, 1996) if greater precision is required, since Voronoi vertices can be recovered from the Delaunay triangulation (Sec. 3.4).

3.3. Voronoi Diagram Construction

Following previous GPU approaches (Ray et al., 2018; Basselin et al., 2021; Taveira et al., 2026a), we represent the Voronoi diagram as an adjacency graph. However, we propose a new algorithm designed specifically for near-centroidal distributions. We assume the sites are in general position as a simplification, this means there are no duplicates and five sites or more are not cospherical.

Cells as linear programs.

The Voronoi cell of the site 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} is:

(6) 𝒞i={𝐱∈ℝ3,||𝐱−𝐱i||22≤||𝐱−𝐱j||22,∀j≠i}.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{i}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{3},||\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{i}||^{2}_{2}\leq||\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{j}||^{2}_{2},\quad\forall j\neq i\}.

Let 𝐱=𝐱i+𝐲\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}_{i}+\mathbf{y}. The distance constraints in equation 6 can be reformulated geometrically as plane equations:

(7) ‖𝐱−𝐱i‖22≤‖𝐱−𝐱j‖22\displaystyle||\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{i}||^{2}_{2}\leq||\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{j}||^{2}_{2}
(8) ⇔\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\quad ‖𝐲‖22≤‖𝐱i+𝐲−𝐱j‖22\displaystyle||\mathbf{y}||^{2}_{2}\leq||\mathbf{x}_{i}+\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}_{j}||^{2}_{2}
(9) ⇔\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\quad ‖𝐲‖22≤‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖22+2​𝐲⋅(𝐱i−𝐱j)+‖𝐲‖22\displaystyle||\mathbf{y}||^{2}_{2}\leq||\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{j}||^{2}_{2}+2\mathbf{y}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{j})+||\mathbf{y}||_{2}^{2}
(10) ⇔\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\quad 𝐲⋅(𝐱j−𝐱i)≤12​‖𝐱j−𝐱i‖22.\displaystyle\mathbf{y}\cdot(\mathbf{x}_{j}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\leq\frac{1}{2}||\mathbf{x}_{j}-\mathbf{x}_{i}||_{2}^{2}.

Therefore, the Voronoi cell is equivalently defined as the feasibility region of a linear program in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}:

(11) 𝒞i={𝐱∈ℝ3,(𝐱−𝐱i)⋅(𝐱j−𝐱i)≤12||𝐱j−𝐱i||22,∀j≠i}.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{i}=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{3},(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\cdot(\mathbf{x}_{j}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\leq\frac{1}{2}||\mathbf{x}_{j}-\mathbf{x}_{i}||^{2}_{2},\quad\forall j\neq i\}.

The Voronoi cell 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} is bounded by a subset of the bisector planes between 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} and its neighboring sites. We call a neighbor 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j} active if its bisector plane with 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} intersects 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}, and the corresponding constraint in (11) contributes to the boundary of 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}. Not all neighboring sites are necessarily active; for example, removing 𝐱k\mathbf{x}_{k} does not change 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} in Fig. 4. Therefore, identifying the set of active neighbors, or equivalently their bisector planes, is sufficient to define the Voronoi cell.

Adjacency as 2D feasibility.

An active bisector plane must contain points of 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} since it corresponds to a facet of the convex polyhedron enclosing the cell. Conversely, inactive bisector planes do not contain any points of the Voronoi cell. This leads to a simple test:

(12) The site ​r​ is a Voronoi neighbor of site ​i\displaystyle\text{The site }r\text{ is a Voronoi neighbor of site }i
(13) ⟺𝒫r is active for cell 𝒞i\displaystyle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\text{$\mathcal{P}_{r}$ is active for cell $\mathcal{C}_{i}$}
(14) ⟺𝒫r∩𝒞i≠∅\displaystyle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\mathcal{P}_{r}\cap\mathcal{C}_{i}\neq\emptyset

We parametrize 𝒫r\mathcal{P}_{r} as 𝐱=12​(𝐱r+𝐱i)+u​𝐞1+v​𝐞2\mathbf{x}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}_{r}+\mathbf{x}_{i})+u\,\mathbf{e}_{1}+v\,\mathbf{e}_{2}, where (𝐞1,𝐞2,(𝐱r−𝐱i)/‖𝐱r−𝐱i‖)(\mathbf{e}_{1},\mathbf{e}_{2},(\mathbf{x}_{r}-\mathbf{x}_{i})/||\mathbf{x}_{r}-\mathbf{x}_{i}||) is an orthonormal basis (Duff et al., 2017). Substituting the parametric equation for 𝒫r\mathcal{P}_{r} into the remaining constraints of Eq. (11) yields a 2D linear program (see Fig. 5):

(15) aj​u+bj​v≤cj,j≠i,j≠r,a_{j}u+b_{j}v\leq c_{j},\qquad j\neq i,\;j\neq r,

and 𝐱r\mathbf{x}_{r} is a neighbor if and only if this system is feasible.

Feasibility test.

We test feasibility with Seidel’s incremental algorithm (Seidel, 1991; Anupam and Danny, 2016), which maintains a feasible point and updates it only when a new constraint is violated, by solving a 1D problem along that constraint’s boundary line. Instead of shuffling the constraints randomly, we process them in increasing distance order, as returned by the KNN kernel (Sec. 3.5). The nearest planes are the most likely to bound the cell, so infeasibility is usually detected early.

GPU implementation.

We consider that only the 32 nearest neighbors are likely to define active bisector planes, so there are 32 threads dedicated for building each cell. Each one tests a candidate plane 𝒫r\mathcal{P}_{r} against the 37 remaining constraints (31 other neighbors and the 6 planes of the scene bounding box). The 2D constraints are built on the fly from the site positions so no per-thread storage is needed, which is a significant bottleneck in previous approaches (Ray et al., 2018; Basselin et al., 2021) due to reduced GPU occupancy. At the end, each thread outputs a single bit classifying whether the neighbor is Voronoi-adjacent.

Approximation.

The assumption that 32 neighbors are enough generally holds in the case of our biased CVT. To further reduce the number of missing adjacencies, we center the KNN queries at the previously computed cell centroids rather than at the sites themselves. This substantially improves the completeness of the resulting Voronoi diagrams, as demonstrated in the supplementary material. More neighbors could be included to handle more irregular cells, though with a performance loss. If a true neighbor beyond the KK nearest sites is missed, the cell will be enlarged and will overlap its neighbor. A missing constraint can also enlarge the feasible region of Eq. (15), so that a non-neighbor is wrongly marked as adjacent. Both errors are local and only affect cells near the few sites concerned.

3.4. Delaunay Triangulation

We convert the approximate Voronoi diagram into the dual Delaunay triangulation for mesh extraction, illustrated in figure 6. For conciseness, "Voronoi neighbor" will be shortened to "neighbor" in the following discussion.

The Delaunay tetrahedra are groups of 4 sites (i,j,k,l)(i,j,k,l) that are pairwise neighbors, and whose circumsphere does not contain any other site. Thus, we enumerate all possible 4-cliques, and then test whether their circumsphere is empty. Only ordered tuples i<j<k<li<j<k<l are emitted to avoid duplicates.

We build a binary adjacency matrix M for each site ii, that encodes the adjacency relation of its neighbors: Mj,kM_{j,k} is 11 if sites jj and kk are neighbors. To form a quadruplet, we look for a neighbor ll of ii such that Mj,lM_{j,l} and Mk,lM_{k,l} are set to 11 in M.

We efficiently enumerate the quadruplets (i,j,k,l)(i,j,k,l) by leveraging the binary nature of M: because each site has 32 neighbors at most, the rows of M can be encoded as 32-bit integers. Thus, jj indices correspond to the direct neighbors of ii, kk indices correspond to the bits set in row MjM_{j}, and ll indices correspond to the bits set in the binary AND of rows MjM_{j} and MkM_{k}. The __ffs CUDA intrinsic lets us iterate over the toggled bits of an integer.

Not all quadruplets form Delaunay tetrahedra so we remove the ones containing other sites in their circumsphere. In practice, we only need to test the neighbors of ii against the circumsphere. A proof is available in the supplementary document.

Because our Voronoi diagram may be incomplete, our triangulation is not guaranteed to be exact for cells with missing clipping planes or in case of numerical ambiguities in the circumsphere check. This can result in a few holes or non-manifold edges in the extracted mesh out of millions of triangles. We quantify these defects in the supplementary material.

3.5. Fast GPU KNN Search

We propose a fast K-nearest neighbor kernel, tailored for K=32K=32 and for repeated queries, to take advantage of our specific setting: the sites move by small amounts between rebuilds of the nearest-neighbors lists, which implies a high degree of temporal consistency that can be leveraged. Like Jakob et al. (Jakob and Guthe, 2021), we start by building an acceleration structure to avoid a naive O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) brute force check. We use a classic LBVH (Lauterbach et al., 2009) with up to 128 points per node. This gives a shallow hierarchy well-suited for querying a relatively large number of neighbors.

The nearest neighbors are gathered using ball-queries, i.e. gathering all points within some distance of the query point, instead of the more common heap-based approach (Jakob and Guthe, 2021; Ray et al., 2018). The ball-query is restarted with a smaller or larger radius until the number of gathered points is between 32 and 64, using a binary search. They are subsequently sorted in increasing distance to the query point (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026) and the first 32 are returned. Each query point has its own search radius which we save for later runs. The point cloud evolves slowly so the search radius is likely to be valid the next time the KNN routine is called, sparing repeated BVH traversals.

Heap-based approaches generally assign one thread per query point, and therefore need a per-thread traversal stack or priority queue, in addition to the heap already required to keep track of the K closest points. While the heap can be stored in registers (Jakob and Guthe, 2021), this reduces occupancy considerably for large values of K or spills the registers to global memory.

Our strategy addresses these issues: we assign one warp per query point, with all lanes visiting the BVH together. A single BVH traversal stack is needed for the whole warp, and the points can be loaded with coalesced memory accesses. The points within the search radius are compacted to a shared memory buffer sorted in parallel at the end, which is faster than iterative heap insertions.

4. Differentiable Volume Rendering

After gathering the nearest neighbors of all sites and computing the Voronoi diagram, we can proceed with rendering of the scene. The volume rendering integral is typically evaluated with ray-marching (Mildenhall et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021), by querying the radiance and density fields at arbitrary locations along the rays. Directly adopting this formulation for our discretization is ill-suited: interpolating point neighborhoods at each ray sample is costly (Xu et al., 2022), while interpolating over the Voronoi cells generally requires a tetrahedral mesh (Thomas et al., 2025; Mai et al., 2026). Instead, we follow RadiantFoam (Govindarajan et al., 2025) and use piecewise integration where each cell only contributes to the portion of the ray it intersects. RadiantFoam (Govindarajan et al., 2025) and SDFoam (Rech et al., 2026) use a constant density inside the cells which does not account for local surface orientation. In comparison, we define the SDF as a linear function in each cell to obtain nonlinearities once composed with NeuS (Wang et al., 2021)’s SDF-to-density conversion, and which crucially still gives a closed-form solution to the volume integral over the ray segments.

Three elements are necessary: (i) the SDF gradient at each site to define a piecewise SDF, (ii) per-primitive radiance and (iii) regularization terms to stabilize optimization. We reuse the nearest neighbors gathered during the Voronoi diagram construction (section 3.5) to regularize the sites’ attributes and to compute the SDF gradient. For view-dependent appearance, we favor a neural implicit approach instead of per-site spherical harmonics to reduce the number of appearance parameters, as explained in section 4.2. Finally, section 4.3 covers our rasterization algorithm designed for small primitives.

4.1. Attributes Smoothing

Smoothing shape and appearance attributes is essential to stabilize optimization and recover sensible geometry in the case of discrete representations (Wu et al., 2023; Toussaint et al., 2025). Here, we leverage ideas from the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) literature to define smoothing operators of arbitrary fields defined at the sites (Price, 2012). These operators are differentiable with respect to spatial coordinates, which in turn enables us to define the gradient of the SDF in a differentiable manner. Let G⁡(u)G(u) be the smoothing operator:

(16) G(u)i=∑j∈𝒩⁡(i)ujwi​j/∑j∈𝒩⁡(i)wi​j.\displaystyle G(u)_{i}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}u_{j}w_{ij}\ \ /\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}w_{ij}.

uu can be any scalar or vector field held by the sites, and G​(u)iG(u)_{i} denotes the smoothed field computed at the position of site ii. 𝒩⁡(i)\mathcal{N}(i) is the set of neighbors of ii, plus ii itself. The smoothing weights are defined as follows:

(17) wi​j\displaystyle w_{ij} =𝒱j​exp⁡(−‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖222​σ2​Ri2)\displaystyle=\mathcal{V}_{j}\exp{\left(-\frac{||\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{j}||_{2}^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}R_{i}^{2}}\right)}
(18) Ri\displaystyle R_{i} =maxj∈𝒩⁡(i)⁡(‖𝐱i−𝐱j‖2).\displaystyle=\max_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)}(||\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{j}||_{2}).

𝒱j\mathcal{V}_{j} is the volume of cell jj and σ\sigma is chosen so that sites further away than the last neighbor would have small weights if they were included. Other smoothing schemes are possible (Koschier et al., 2020; Koschier et al., 2019) but we found this simple one to be effective. The weights wi​jw_{ij} take the cell volume into account so that GG approximates the convolution of the field uu by a Gaussian kernel:

(19) (u⁡(𝐲)∗e−‖𝐲‖22​σ2​R2)​(𝐱)\displaystyle(u(\mathbf{y})*e^{-\frac{||\mathbf{y}||^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}R^{2}}})(\mathbf{x}) =∫ℝ3u⁡(𝐲)​exp⁡(−‖𝐱−𝐲‖22​σ2​R2)​𝑑𝐲\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}u(\mathbf{y})\exp{\left(-\frac{||\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}||^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}R^{2}}\right)}d\mathbf{y}
(20) ≈∑juj​exp⁡(−‖𝐱−𝐱j‖22​σ2​R2)​𝒱j.\displaystyle\approx\sum_{j}u_{j}\exp{\left(-\frac{||\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{j}||^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}R^{2}}\right)}\mathcal{V}_{j}.

Equation 20 is the Riemann sum of the integral discretized over all the sites, that we further divide by the sum of the weights to normalize GG. Following (Wu et al., 2023; Toussaint et al., 2025), we apply our Gaussian filter GG on the raw SDF ff to obtain smoother values:

(21) f^=G⁡(f)\displaystyle\hat{f}=G(f)

Next, we obtain the gradient vector of the smoothed SDF by computing partial derivatives of GG applied on f^\hat{f}:

(22) 𝐧i\displaystyle\mathbf{n}_{i} =∇𝐱iG​(f^)i.\displaystyle=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{i}}G(\hat{f})_{i}.

We are now able to define regularization objectives typically used in multi-view implicit surface reconstruction:

(23) ℒSDF\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{SDF}} =∑i(fi−f^i)2max⁡(|sg⁡(f^i)|,0.01)\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{(f_{i}-\hat{f}_{i})^{2}}{\max(|\operatorname{sg}\!\left(\hat{f}_{i}\right)|,0.01)}
(24) ℒ𝐧\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{n}} =∑i‖𝐧i‖𝐧i‖2−sg⁡(G⁡(𝐧i‖𝐧i‖2))‖22\displaystyle=\sum_{i}||\frac{\mathbf{n}_{i}}{||\mathbf{n}_{i}||_{2}}-\operatorname{sg}\!\left(G(\frac{\mathbf{n}_{i}}{||\mathbf{n}_{i}||_{2}})\right)||_{2}^{2}
(25) ℒEik\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{Eik}} =∑i(‖𝐧i‖2−1)2\displaystyle=\sum_{i}(||\mathbf{n}_{i}||_{2}-1)^{2}

ℒSDF\mathcal{L}_{\text{SDF}} keeps ff and f^\hat{f} close to each other, ℒ𝐧\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{n}} is a smoothness term on the normalized gradient vectors and ℒEik\mathcal{L}_{\text{Eik}} is the classic eikonal regularization (Gropp et al., 2020). sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}\!\left(\cdot\right) is the stop gradient operator added to simplify the backward pass. Furthermore, we do not back-propagate loss gradients through the positions of the sites, by treating them as constants in this formulation: their positions are entirely managed by the CVT loss defined in section 3.1.

So far, the SDF was only defined at the sites. We extend it to an entire Voronoi cell using an affine approximation:

(26) f^​(𝐱)=f^i+(𝐱−𝐱i)⋅𝐧i,∀𝐱∈𝒞i.\displaystyle\hat{f}(\mathbf{x})=\hat{f}_{i}+(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i},\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{C}_{i}.

When considering all the cells, the signed-distance field will be piecewise linear with small discontinuities allowed between cells. The affine approximations let us obtain a closed-form solution to the volume rendering integral, as described in section 4.3, which may not be possible with typical interpolation schemes.

4.2. Appearance Representation

We assign a view-dependent color to each cell 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} to model the scene appearance. Like 3DGS (Kerbl et al., 2023), the color is constant inside a primitive, which gives a piecewise constant color field in our case. Our appearance parametrization takes inspiration from (Toussaint et al., 2025). The main idea is to split view-independent components (e.g. texture) from view-dependent components of the light field (e.g. shading) to significantly reduce the number of parameters compared to a distinct spherical harmonic (SH) basis per primitive.

The view-independent component is parametrized by a feature vector 𝐅is∈ℝ4\mathbf{F}_{i}^{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}, called the spatial features, assigned to each site. The view-dependent component is modeled by a dense voxel grid of spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients called the light probes. They are trilinearly interpolated at the location of the sites to produce a per-primitive SH basis, subsequently evaluated in the direction of a unit vector to obtain angular features 𝐅ia∈ℝ4\mathbf{F}_{i}^{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}. More specifically, we use two sets of light probes: the first one is queried with the incident vector 𝐯\mathbf{v} and the other uses the reflected vector 𝐰\mathbf{w}, which give 𝐅ia,𝐯\mathbf{F}_{i}^{a,\mathbf{v}} and 𝐅ia,𝐰\mathbf{F}_{i}^{a,\mathbf{w}} respectively. The site color 𝐜i\mathbf{c}_{i} is obtained by decoding the spatial and angular features with a tiny MLP:

(27) 𝐜i=MLP​(𝐅is,𝐅ia,𝐯,𝐅ia,𝐰,(𝐧i⋅𝐯i)1,⋯,(𝐧i⋅𝐯i)4)\displaystyle\mathbf{c}_{i}=\text{MLP}(\mathbf{F}_{i}^{s},\mathbf{F}_{i}^{a,\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{F}_{i}^{a,\mathbf{w}},(\mathbf{n}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{i})^{1},\cdots,(\mathbf{n}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{i})^{4})

For regularization, we add a smoothness term on the spatial features, similar to the smoothness term on the normals:

(28) ℒ𝐅s=∑i‖𝐅is−sg⁡(G⁡(𝐅is))‖22\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{F}^{s}}=\sum_{i}||\mathbf{F}_{i}^{s}-\operatorname{sg}\!\left(G(\mathbf{F}_{i}^{s})\right)||_{2}^{2}

The light probes are also regularized by applying a Gaussian filter 𝒢\mathcal{G} on the voxels and penalizing deviations between the smoothed and raw coefficients:

(29) ℒprobes=∑‖β−sg⁡(𝒢⁡(β))‖22\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{probes}}=\sum||\beta-\operatorname{sg}\!\left(\mathcal{G}(\beta)\right)||_{2}^{2}

The sum is applied on all the voxels and SH basis coefficients β\beta.

In practice, the two voxel grids have resolution 32332^{3}, with 16 SH coefficients per voxel and each SH coefficient in ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4}. The MLP has 16 neurons with 2 hidden layers and squareplus activations (Barron, 2021). Because there are multiple sites located in the same voxel in general, the light probes represent a small proportion of all parameters (equivalent to ≈1\approx 1 parameter per primitive in our experiments).

4.3. Real-Time Rasterization

The scene is ready to be rasterized into an image once every site has been assigned a color for the current camera position. We use NeuS’ rendering equation (Wang et al., 2021) with reciprocal transmittance (Miller et al., 2024) to blend colors along a camera ray 𝐨+t​𝐫,t>0\mathbf{o}+t\mathbf{r},t>0:

(30) 𝐂\displaystyle\mathbf{C} =∫0+∞𝐜⁡(t)​σ​(t)​T​(0,t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\mathbf{c}(t)\sigma(t)T(0,t)dt
(31) T⁡(0,t)\displaystyle T(0,t) =e−∫0tσ(u)du\displaystyle=e^{-\int_{0}^{t}\sigma(u)du}
(32) σ⁡(t)\displaystyle\sigma(t) =s​Φ​(−s​f^​(t))​|𝐧⋅𝐫|\displaystyle=s\Phi(-s\hat{f}(t))|\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{r}|

Φ\Phi is the sigmoid function and s>0s>0 is the sharpness parameter controlling the density decay outside of the implicit surface. In the equations above, 𝐜⁡(t)=𝐜⁡(𝐨+t​𝐫)\mathbf{c}(t)=\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{o}+t\mathbf{r}), σ⁡(t)=σ⁡(𝐨+t​𝐫)\sigma(t)=\sigma(\mathbf{o}+t\mathbf{r}), etc.

Because the color is constant inside a cell and the SDF is piecewise linear (see figure 8), and by further assuming the cells do not overlap which is typically the case, we obtain a closed-form solution for equation 30. Complete derivations are provided in the supplementary document, we give the final formula below:

(33) 𝐂\displaystyle\mathbf{C} =∑𝐜i​(1−αi)​∏j<iαj\displaystyle=\sum\mathbf{c}_{i}(1-\alpha_{i})\prod_{j<i}\alpha_{j}
(34) αi\displaystyle\alpha_{i} =1+e−s​f^​(ti−)1+e−s​f^​(ti+)∈[0,1]\displaystyle=\frac{1+e^{-s\hat{f}(t_{i}^{-})}}{1+e^{-s\hat{f}(t_{i}^{+})}}\in[0,1]

We use the convention that α\alpha corresponds to the transparency of the cell. f^​(ti−)\hat{f}(t_{i}^{-}) and f^​(ti+)\hat{f}(t_{i}^{+}) are the piecewise SDF (equation 26) evaluated at the entry and exit points of the ray in the cell respectively. The sum in equation 33 is carried over the set of Voronoi cells intersected by the ray, ordered by increasing distance to the camera to guarantee geometrically-consistent blending (not depth, see (Govindarajan et al., 2026) for a proof). Note that the fraction in eq. 34 should be inverted for back-facing cells so that α≤1\alpha\leq 1.

In practice, we first assign each cell to every 8×88\times 8 pixel tile intersected by the projection of its bounding sphere, sort them by tile id and by distance, and then evaluate equation 33.

4.3.1. Chunked Rasterizer

We noticed using one thread per ray results in poor GPU utilization whenever some rays intersect more cells than the average, which occurs for grazing rays that are parallel to the surface. In the worst case, a single thread can keep the GPU busy while the rest have terminated long before.

Thus, we propose to split the sum in equation 33 into contiguous ranges of 32 cells that we call chunks, with the goal of increasing parallelism during rasterization.

As figure 9 shows, all chunks are scheduled to be processed in parallel, with chunks closer to the camera being handled first since we order them front-to-back. Naively processing the chunks all at once is not ideal because occluded cells would still be intersected and blended. In comparison, a sequential processing can exit as soon as the per-ray transmittance reaches zero. To retain this useful behavior, we propose a communication system based on per-pixel flags that are updated atomically by the chunks when they terminate their local rasterization task.

Each flag contains a transmittance accumulator TcT_{c} and a distance counter DcD_{c}, updated jointly with an atomic compare-and-swap. TcT_{c} corresponds to the multiplication of the partial transmittance values of the chunks having completed so far. The distance counter DcD_{c} contains the (depth) index of the furthest completed chunk. When a chunk starts, it reads the flags of its 8x8 pixel tile and decides if rasterization is needed based on the following table:

Early-exit decision table Tc≥ϵT_{c}\geq\epsilon TcT_{c} < ϵ\epsilon
chunk index < DcD_{c} Cannot skip Cannot skip
chunk index > DcD_{c} Cannot skip Can skip

Rasterization is skipped if all rays in the chunk can skip. The accumulator TcT_{c} is an upper bound of the true transmittance up to chunk DcD_{c}, valid for all chunks with depth index i≥Dci\geq D_{c}. It is an upper bound since earlier chunks may not have updated TcT_{c} when further ones read it. Therefore, a low value for TcT_{c} guarantees that further chunks will not contribute to the final color. On the other hand, chunks closer than the distance counter have to run regardless of TcT_{c}. This scheme allows chunks pertaining to the same pixel tile to be processed fully in parallel if the GPU has enough thread blocks available, while hidden chunks will be opportunistically skipped. A distinct GPU kernel performs the final blending of each chunk’s output color and transmittance in a later pass.

The main cost in evaluating equation 33 is the computation of the ray/cell intersection intervals (ti−,ti+)(t_{i}^{-},t_{i}^{+}) due to execution divergence: each ray intersects a different subset of cells. To reduce this cost, we let threads work on different cells concurrently. The alternative is to iterate over the cells sequentially, and only the threads whose ray intersects the current cell can make progress while the others are inactive. For a given chunk, we first load the attributes of its 32 cells cooperatively in shared memory.

Then, each thread performs a ray/sphere intersection test (Haines et al., 2019) against the cells’ bounding spheres, which produces a bit mask with one bit per cell. This part is sequential but relatively inexpensive. Next, each thread iterates over the bits set in its intersection mask and performs the more expensive ray/cell check against the corresponding cell, which need not be the same for all threads. The maximum number of bits set in the mask across threads determines the total number of iterations, often lower than 3232 since a ray is unlikely to intersect all cells’ bounding spheres in the chunk. This optimization makes sense in our case because the cells are only a few pixels across and intersection tests are costly. Larger primitives would not benefit as much because more rays intersect them at once, and thus incur lower execution divergence.

The bisector planes are encoded as vectors 𝐩ik∈ℝ3\mathbf{p}_{i}^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, whose direction is the plane normal, oriented away from the site, and with length equal to the distance between the site and the plane.

(35) ti−\displaystyle t_{i}^{-} =maxk𝐩ik⋅𝐫<0⁡∥𝐩ik∥22−(𝐨−𝐱i)⋅𝐩ik𝐫⋅𝐩ik,\displaystyle=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\\ \mathbf{p}_{i}^{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}<0\end{subarray}}\frac{\lVert\mathbf{p}_{i}^{k}\rVert_{2}^{2}-(\mathbf{o}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\cdot\mathbf{p}_{i}^{k}}{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{i}^{k}},
(36) ti+\displaystyle t_{i}^{+} =mink𝐩ik⋅𝐫>0⁡∥𝐩ik∥22−(𝐨−𝐱i)⋅𝐩ik𝐫⋅𝐩ik.\displaystyle=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\\ \mathbf{p}_{i}^{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{\lVert\mathbf{p}_{i}^{k}\rVert_{2}^{2}-(\mathbf{o}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\cdot\mathbf{p}_{i}^{k}}{\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{i}^{k}}.

If ti−≥ti+t_{i}^{-}\geq t_{i}^{+}, this indicates the ray does not intersect the cell.

5. Optimization and Implementation

5.1. Color remapping

The rendered color 𝐂\mathbf{C} in equation 33 is further composited with background pixel values sampled from a trainable envmap at infinity: 𝐂2=𝐂+𝐂env​T\mathbf{C}_{2}=\mathbf{C}+\mathbf{C}_{\text{env}}T, with T=∏αiT=\prod\alpha_{i} the transmittance. We use an octahedral mapping to parametrize the envmap (Cigolle et al., 2014), with a resolution of 102421024^{2}. Then, the color is tone-mapped to the [0,1][0,1] interval: 𝐂3=𝐂2/(𝐂2+1.0)\mathbf{C}_{3}=\mathbf{C}_{2}/(\mathbf{C}_{2}+1.0), before applying a trainable color correction curve: 𝐂final=γ⁡(𝐂3)\mathbf{C}_{\text{final}}=\gamma(\mathbf{C}_{3}). The color correction curve is a piecewise linear ramp mapping the [0,1][0,1] interval to itself, distinct for each color channel and each camera (Toussaint et al., 2025).

5.2. Image Losses

Our data term is a weighted combination of a normalized L2 loss, a mask loss, a structural loss and a multi-view loss. We also add an L1 smoothing term on the depth, taken as the first intersection with the implicit surface.

(37) ℒRGB\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{RGB}} =∑‖𝐂final−𝐂gt‖2​Mmax⁡(𝐂gt,0.01)\displaystyle=\sum||\mathbf{C}_{\text{final}}-\mathbf{C}_{\text{gt}}||^{2}\frac{M}{\max{(\mathbf{C}_{\text{gt}},0.01)}}
(38) ℒMask\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{Mask}} =∑(T−(1−M))2\displaystyle=\sum(T-(1-M))^{2}
(39) ℒDSSIM\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSSIM}} =∑(1−SSIM​(𝐂final,𝐂gt))​M\displaystyle=\sum(1-\text{SSIM}(\mathbf{C}_{\text{final}},\mathbf{C}_{\text{gt}}))M
(40) ℒMV\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{MV}} =∑(1−ZNCC)\displaystyle=\sum(1-\text{ZNCC})
(41) ℒD\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{D} =∑|d−sg⁡(d¯)|\displaystyle=\sum|d-\operatorname{sg}\!\left(\bar{d}\right)|

𝐂gt\mathbf{C}_{\text{gt}} is the ground truth image, MM is the mask, TT is the transmittance, ZNCC is the cross-correlation computed on pairs of nearby viewpoints, dd is the depth and d¯\bar{d} is the averaged depth of the neighboring pixels. The sums are applied to all the pixels of the cameras in the mini-batch. We use coarse-to-fine supervision from the ground truth images, with four levels of detail in total. Our complete optimization objective is a weighted combination of all the losses:

ℒ\displaystyle\mathcal{L} =λRGB​ℒRGB+λMask​ℒMask+λDSSIM​ℒDSSIM\displaystyle=\lambda_{\text{RGB}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{RGB}}+\lambda_{\text{Mask}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{Mask}}+\lambda_{\text{DSSIM}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSSIM}}
+λMV​ℒMV+λD​ℒD+λCVT​ℒCVT\displaystyle\quad+\lambda_{\text{MV}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{MV}}+\lambda_{D}\mathcal{L}_{D}+\lambda_{\text{CVT}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{CVT}}
+λSDF​ℒSDF+λ𝐧​ℒ𝐧+λEik​ℒEik\displaystyle\quad+\lambda_{\text{SDF}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{SDF}}+\lambda_{\mathbf{n}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{n}}+\lambda_{\text{Eik}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{Eik}}
(42) +λprobes​ℒprobes+λ𝐅s​ℒ𝐅s.\displaystyle\quad+\lambda_{\text{probes}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{probes}}+\lambda_{\mathbf{F}^{s}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{F}^{s}}.

We propose to additionally weigh the image-loss gradients per-primitive during the backward pass based on their projected size. This re-weighting makes the training seamless when the resolution of the training images is switched to the next level of detail in the coarse-to-fine pyramid.

(43) rproj\displaystyle r_{\text{proj}} =r​fx/z\displaystyle=rf_{x}/z
(44) gmod\displaystyle g_{\text{mod}} =1/rproj2\displaystyle=1/r_{\text{proj}}^{2}

rr is the radius of the cell’s bounding sphere, fxf_{x} is the focal length and zz is the depth of the site for the current viewpoint. gmodg_{\text{mod}} is the per-primitive weight.

5.3. Initialization and Densification

Initially, we spread the sites in the scene bounding box based on a uniform distribution and apply 10 iterations of Lloyd’s relaxation to uniformize the cells (a=0a=0 in equation 1). The SDF is initialized from a sphere, while the rest of the learnable features are randomized based on a normal distribution.

We start with 200K sites, and increase their number every 10 iterations until we reach 4M sites by following a geometric progression. To place new sites, we pick a random viewpoint and render a depth map and a feature map. The feature map is the α\alpha-blending of the sites’ spatial features 𝐅s\mathbf{F}^{s}. A new site is placed at the depth sampled from a random valid pixel in the depth map, and its feature vector 𝐅s\mathbf{F}^{s} is sampled from the same pixel in the feature map.

The nearest-neighbors list is rebuilt each time new points are added, while the Voronoi diagram is recomputed more frequently: at each iteration in the beginning, and every five iterations towards the end. We train for 10K iterations, with four training images per mini-batch. New points are added starting from the 400th iteration, until the last 400 iterations. For the last 400 iterations, we replace the planar-based ZNCC with a nonplanar version to avoid suppressing fine-scale details. More details regarding the multi-view loss and the weight scheduling are given in the supplementary material.

6. Experimental validation

All experiments in this section used a workstation equipped with an RTX 5090 GPU and an Intel Core Ultra 7 265K with 20 cores to measure timings, with the exception of table 2 where we report each method’s timing and corresponding hardware configuration. Best, second and third best results are highlighted in the tables.

6.1. Multi-view Reconstruction

Evaluation on DTU. We evaluate the multi-view reconstruction accuracy of our approach on 15 scenes from the DTU dataset (Aanæs et al., 2016). Quantitative results are reported in table 2 and qualitative results are shown in figure 10. We achieve state-of-the-art geometric accuracy, tied with GGGS (Zhang et al., 2026b) and BlobsToSpokes (Gomez et al., 2026), while requiring a training time of approximately 2.5 minutes. Our approach reproduces high-frequency geometric details that GGGS and BlobsToSpokes miss, this is particularly noticeable in the close-ups on scans 24 and 106 shown at the top of fig. 10. We hypothesize the qualitative improvement does not lead to quantitative improvement due to noise in the ground truth point clouds and down-sampling of the input reconstructions by the official evaluation script.

For consistency with the 3DGS-like approaches (Huang et al., 2024), we discard vertices that project outside of the training masks as well as hidden vertices before Chamfer distance evaluation, since closed surfaces tend to be penalized under the DTU evaluation protocol.

Evaluation on BlendedMVS. We also compare our approach on 8 scenes from the BlendedMVS (Yao et al., 2020) dataset in table 1, with qualitative results presented in figure 11. We measure Chamfer distances as point-to-mesh distances in the normalized reference frame used for training, with the same evaluation protocol on this dataset as ProbeSDF (Toussaint et al., 2025). The images were cropped before running PGSR and GGGS according to the 2DGS protocol (Huang et al., 2024), since they require a projection center in the middle of the images. We achieve high geometric accuracy using the same hyperparameters as on DTU, with GGGS slightly ahead quantitatively but with noticeable noise (see figure 11). PGSR fails to produce a mesh in two instances due to ambiguous white backgrounds which caused the GPU to run out of memory during mesh extraction.

Additional evaluations of photometric accuracy are provided in the supplementary material.

6.2. Training Speed Analysis on DTU

We evaluate in table 3 the two main configuration hyperparameters of our approach: the number of sites and the number of training iterations. Reducing either of these produces a small decrease in accuracy but lowers training time substantially. Qualitative results are shown in figure 12.

Next, using the chunked rasterizer described in section 4.3.1 has the largest impact on runtime: the optimization takes 147147s with it, compared to 280280s using a baseline that assigns a single GPU thread per pixel similarly to 3DGS (Kerbl et al., 2023). This almost gives a 2×2\times speedup on the end-to-end optimization. Both rasterizers achieve nearly the same Chamfer distance and the remaining discrepancy can likely be attributed to differences in floating-point arithmetic.

6.3. Ablations on DTU

We ablate our losses and regularization terms in table 4, ordered by decreasing importance. Figure 13 compares against the base model qualitatively. Training using a linear radiance tone-mapped after rasterization, compared to a typical sigmoid-bounded nonlinear radiance, avoids a failure case on scan 65 due to large patches of saturated pixels, but makes little difference otherwise. Removing the multi-view loss (No ZNCC) or the depth smoothing loss has a strong impact overall. Setting a=0.05a=0.05 in the biased CVT loss (eq. 1), instead of a=0.10a=0.10 prevents the cells from shrinking sufficiently which reduces accuracy but does not create hard failure cases. The reflection probes are important for recovering smooth geometry in specular regions (scan 110, 69). Adding an environment map helps compensating for slight inaccuracies in the supervision masks (scan 83). The rest of the components have lower importance: the SSIM, color correction curves and view probes are added for robustness against inconsistent illumination conditions. Removing one of them does not affect geometry meaningfully. Finishing training with the non planar ZNCC term instead of the planar ZNCC gives a qualitative improvement in fine details (scan 106). Finally, removing the normal smoothing term (eq. 24) slightly improves the Chamfer distance compared to our base model but also introduces artifacts (scan 110). The gradient modulation (eq. 44) does not change the end result but makes training more stable.

6.4. KNN Efficiency

We measure the speed of our KNN (K=32) implementation against five baselines on the 4M points DTU checkpoints and present the results in table 5. For our approach, we distinguish between the case where the ball query search radius is already known (w. warmup) compared to when it is unknown which takes approximately 3×3\times longer. In practice, most of the sites can rely on the search radius used in the KNN lookup of the previous training iteration.

MeshlessVoronoi (Ray et al., 2018) and RestrictedVoronoi (Basselin et al., 2021) use the same strategy so we only discuss (Basselin et al., 2021) which was slightly faster. The input points are partitioned on a dense voxel grid as a pre-process. Then, each query point visits the voxels in concentric rings and keeps track of the KNN using a heap in shared memory. Importantly, we doubled their hard-coded maximum search radius to accommodate our adaptive point distributions, otherwise these baselines fail to gather all requested neighbors.

CuPy-KNN (Igelbrink, ) is a re-implementation of (Jakob and Guthe, 2021), based on a BVH and using a heap stored in the registers. Torch-kdtree (Grandits, ) works similarly to Cupy-KNN but builds its acceleration structure on the CPU. Overall, the heap-based approaches are much less efficient than our gather-then-sort approach, even more so when temporal consistency is leveraged. TrueKNN (Nagarajan et al., 2023) relies on the RT cores of the GPU to benefit from hardware-accelerated BVH traversal. This strategy is effective for uniform point distributions but under performs on our point clouds since several retries are needed for low-density regions. We also include scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) as a CPU reference.

6.5. Voronoi and Delaunay Efficiency

We compare the speed of our algorithm for Voronoi diagram construction against five GPU baselines in table 6 and in figure 14, on the 4M points DTU checkpoints. Paragram (Taveira et al., 2026a), gDel3D (Cao et al., 2014) and RadiantFoam (Govindarajan et al., 2025) only output the Voronoi adjacency graph. Closer to our approach, MeshlessVoronoi (Ray et al., 2018) and RestrictedVoronoi (Basselin et al., 2021) produce a list of KNN and also compute cell centroids. We ran both of them with single-precision arithmetic and K=32 neighbors, equivalently to our setting. In the case of RestrictedVoronoi (Basselin et al., 2021), we only report the first round of KNN gathering which corresponds to what we are doing. Subsequent retries with larger K for incomplete cells increase their runtime by about 1.5×1.5\times. The reported timing for our approach assumes the KNN search radius is known, to match the typical case encountered during optimization. Overall, our approach is consistently 5×5\times faster than (Ray et al., 2018) and 10×10\times faster than (Taveira et al., 2026a) in this context, and scales linearly.

For mesh extraction, we convert the adjacency graph into a Delaunay triangulation (sec. 3.4) and subsequently apply marching tetrahedra on the smoothed SDF f^\hat{f}. It is sufficient to only generate the tetrahedra that cross the zero level set, which divides the total mesh extraction time by 3×3\times according to table 7. The zero level set is extracted as a triangle soup for real-time visualization during training. The duplicate vertices are merged on the CPU before outputting the final mesh on disk, which takes two seconds in total.

7. Limitations and Future Work

A limitation of our Voronoi diagram construction algorithm is its approximate nature, which makes it unsuitable for applications requiring exact adjacencies. Iterative retries with a larger number of neighbors in the spirit of Basselin et al. (Basselin et al., 2021) could recover the missing adjacencies. A fallback to double precision could also improve robustness in degenerate configurations.

As evaluated in the supplementary material, we find the proportion of incomplete cells to be low in practice for our choice of hyperparameters. More aggressive adaptivity could be balanced using a larger number of neighbors but at an increased cost. Deriving theoretical upper bounds on the required number of neighbors based on cell regularity (Hudson et al., 2006) could be useful but may be inapplicable in our case since we make no guarantee on sites spacing.

Extending our adaptive discretization to open scenes is an interesting direction for future research. The main obstacles are our naive sphere initialization and the potential lack of scalability for representing geometric and photometric details over large spatial extents. The former could be addressed using monocular priors (Li et al., 2026) and the latter could benefit from adaptive densification based on image content (Kerbl et al., 2023; Govindarajan et al., 2025), or primitives with greater expressivity (Taveira et al., 2026b).

8. Conclusion

We have presented CVTSplat, an approach for multi-view reconstruction combining adaptive Voronoi tessellations with differentiable implicit surface modeling. Our centroidal regularization plays a central role: beyond producing well-shaped cells, it enables us to specialize several components of the pipeline for efficiency. In particular, we introduced a Voronoi diagram construction algorithm that exploits the regularity of the tessellation. We further tailored neighbor queries, centroid computation, rasterization and mesh extraction to our representation. Together, these developments yield a highly efficient pipeline that achieves geometric accuracy competitive with the state-of-the-art on two object-level reconstruction benchmarks.

Appendix A Overview

This supplementary document provides additional implementation details, experiments, derivations and proofs. We report the optimization schedule (section B) followed by statistics on our adaptive Voronoi tessellation: study of mesh defects (section C), accuracy of cell moments computation (section D), frequency of incomplete cells and relationship between cell size and SDF (section E). Evaluations of rendering speed, photometric accuracy and model size are available in sections F, G and H respectively. Section I gives details regarding the multi-view loss and section J concludes with proofs omitted from the main paper.

Appendix B Hyperparameters Scheduling

Our optimization schedule is detailed in table 8.

Appendix C Mesh Defects Analysis

Table 9 reports the average number of topological errors in our extracted meshes. We count the number of non-manifold edges, i.e. edges having more than two incident triangles, and boundary edges that have a single incident triangle. The implicit surface touches the bounding box walls in some scenes, which creates legitimate boundary edges. Therefore, we only count the ones within 95%95\% of the bounding box that actually correspond to small holes in the extracted meshes. Missing Voronoi adjacencies can prevent the formation of tetrahedra and produce small holes, where a single triangle is missing in general. Non-manifold edges may result from inconsistent tetrahedron selection near degenerate configurations or from incomplete Voronoi neighbor lists. Overall, these defects are infrequent relative to the number of mesh triangles and could potentially be addressed by topological post-processing.

Appendix D Cell Moments Estimation

We evaluate in Figure 15 the accuracy of the quadrature formulas for cell volume and centroid using varying numbers of rays sampled on a Fibonacci sphere lattice. Errors are relative and computed with respect to a reference using 81928192 rays. Volume and radius errors are relative to their reference values while the centroid error corresponds to the centroid displacement divided by the reference cell radius. The radius is estimated from the maximum sampled distance to the cell boundary over the set of ray directions. The error curves for the volume and centroid are nearly overlapped and decrease as 1/N1/N, where NN is the number of rays. The radius error decreases more slowly, approximately as 1/N1/\sqrt{N}.

With our default of 64 rays, the mean errors are 0.79%0.79\% for the volume, 0.77%0.77\% for the centroid, and 5.65%5.65\% for the radius. The cell radius mainly serves to define an approximate bounding sphere during rasterization. A more accurate value could be computed using the maximum distance to the circumcenters of incident tetrahedra (i.e. the Voronoi vertices), but that would require computing the Delaunay triangulation from the adjacency graph every time it is updated which would add some overhead. Our approximate bounding spheres only clip the furthest corners of the cells, that would not contribute significantly to the volume integral if included.

Appendix E Distribution of cells

Figure 16 presents statistics about the number of Voronoi neighbors and their distribution within the KNN list. This test used 64 nearest neighbors instead of 32 for validation. A small proportion of cells has Voronoi neighbors beyond the 32nd nearest neighbor (≈0.1%\approx 0.1\%). Extracting the KNN at the centroid decreases that rate substantially (≈0.0006%\approx 0.0006\%) but has little importance on multi-view optimization in practice. Incomplete cells are typically located away from the implicit surface and therefore do not participate in volume rendering or mesh extraction. Nevertheless, we use the offset KNN strategy by default as it provides lower error rates at no additional cost.

Figure 17 explores the relationship between cell size and signed distance induced by our adaptive CVT. The bounding box used for training spans the unit cube [−1,+1]3[-1,+1]^{3}, the SDF and cell radius are given in this reference frame. We find an approximately affine relationship between cell radius and SDF, with most of the cells located close to the implicit surface.

Figure 18 illustrates the sensitivity of the point distribution to the hyperparameter aa in the CVT loss.

Appendix F Rendering speed

Table 10 reports the average size of the primitives once projected to the training views. Each primitive is weighted by its volume rendering weight to compute this metric. We also report the time taken to render an image from the dataset, averaged over all viewpoints and scenes. The timings are measured on an RTX 5090 GPU. The renderings are written to an offscreen buffer so a small additional overhead would be needed in practice to display the result.

Appendix G Photometric Evaluation

We evaluate the photometric accuracy of our approach in table 11, on all available viewpoints and within the silhouette masks eroded by two pixels. All tested methods were trained using all viewpoints so this experiment measures fitting error rather than novel view synthesis fidelity. PGSR (Chen et al., 2024) and GGGS (Zhang et al., 2026b) train on cropped images so we evaluate our method in the same setting for consistency. PGSR and GGGS used half-resolution images on DTU, following their training setup, so we upscale their renderings before evaluation. Our method achieves an image quality comparable to PGSR but slightly below GGGS, with a larger gap on BlendedMVS.

Qualitative comparisons on DTU and BlendedMVS are shown in figures 19 and 20 respectively. We picked viewpoints for which our error is highest compared to GGGS to understand the limitations of our appearance model. The texture is generally well-reproduced in our case but some specular regions are missing due to the SH bases being shared by multiple sites.

Appendix H Model size

Table 12 presents a comparison of our model in terms of number of primitives and number of trainable parameters, compared to PGSR (Chen et al., 2024) and GGGS (Zhang et al., 2026b). Despite using more primitives than GGGS, we have a similar total parameter count on DTU, and lower on BlendedMVS. Table 13 provides a breakdown of parameter usage for our approach.

Appendix I Details on the Multiview Loss

We use a multi-view loss inspired by PGSR (Chen et al., 2024). Pairs of views that are close to each other are chosen at random during training (a mini-batch contains 44 views so that pairs can be formed). During the forward pass of volume rendering, the depth of the first zero-crossing of the SDF is recorded for each ray to form a depth map.

I.1. Depth Computation

For a cell 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} having SDF f^i\hat{f}_{i}, position 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} and SDF gradient 𝐧i\mathbf{n}_{i}, we have the following approximation:

(45) f^​(𝐱)=f^i+(𝐱−𝐱i)⋅𝐧i\displaystyle\hat{f}(\mathbf{x})=\hat{f}_{i}+(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i}

Then for a ray 𝐫⁡(t)=𝐨+t​𝐯\mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{o}+t\mathbf{v}, the zero-crossing is obtained by solving f^​(𝐫​(t∗))=0\hat{f}(\mathbf{r}(t^{*}))=0:

(46) f^i+(𝐨+t∗​𝐯−𝐱i)⋅𝐧i=0\displaystyle\hat{f}_{i}+(\mathbf{o}+t^{*}\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i}=0
(47) ⇔f^i+(𝐨−𝐱i)⋅𝐧i+t∗​𝐯⋅𝐧i=0\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\hat{f}_{i}+(\mathbf{o}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i}+t^{*}\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i}=0
(48) ⇔t∗=−(f^i+(𝐨−𝐱i)⋅𝐧i)/𝐯⋅𝐧i\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow t^{*}=-(\hat{f}_{i}+(\mathbf{o}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i})/\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n}_{i}

The depth value t∗t^{*} is discarded if the point 𝐫⁡(t∗)\mathbf{r}(t^{*}) falls outside of the cell, indicating that the implicit surface does not cross it. There may be several zero-crossings along a given ray, so the final depth value is taken as the minimum over the intersected cells. In case no zero-crossing occurs, we use t∗=+∞t^{*}=+\infty.

Once a depth map is obtained for both views in the pair, we can compute our multi-view loss. We implement two variants based on the zero-normalized cross-correlation (ZNCC). The first one is similar to prior works (Chen et al., 2024; Gomez et al., 2026) based on planar patches, whereas the other removes the planar assumption to recover finer details.

I.2. Planar ZNCC

Let the pair of views be denoted as (A,B)(A,B), with AA the reference view and BB the neighboring view. We compute a normal vector for each pixel (u,v)(u,v) in view AA using centered finite differences in the depth map 𝒟A\mathcal{D}_{A}. Let 𝐧\mathbf{n} be the normal vector expressed in AA’s reference frame. Pixels having invalid depth values (+∞+\infty) or invalid neighboring pixels are skipped. We check for visibility in view BB using a cycle consistency check (same as PGSR (Chen et al., 2024)):

(49) dA\displaystyle d_{A} =𝒟A​(uA,vA)\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{A}(u_{A},v_{A})
(50) uB,vB\displaystyle u_{B},v_{B} =πB​(πA−1​(uA,vA,dA))\displaystyle=\pi_{B}(\pi_{A}^{-1}(u_{A},v_{A},d_{A}))
(51) dB\displaystyle d_{B} =𝒟B​(uB,vB)\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{B}(u_{B},v_{B})
(52) uA′,vA′\displaystyle u_{A}^{\prime},v_{A}^{\prime} =πA​(πB−1​(uB,vB,dB))\displaystyle=\pi_{A}(\pi_{B}^{-1}(u_{B},v_{B},d_{B}))

π\pi denotes the projection operator, mapping 3D points to pixel coordinates and π−1\pi^{-1} its inverse that maps a pixel and depth value back to a 3D point. We consider the pixel to be occluded in view BB if (uA−uA′)2+(vA−vA′)2>2\sqrt{(u_{A}-u_{A}^{\prime})^{2}+(v_{A}-v_{A}^{\prime})^{2}}>2. The pixel may be rejected if the cycle consistency check fails due to the point projecting outside of BB’s field of view, or if the depth in view B is invalid. Lastly, we also check that the normal is not too slanted in either view, with a rejection threshold of 8585° between the normal and the viewing ray.

If these checks pass, we compute the ZNCC over a 5×55\times 5 pixel patch centered on the pixel of interest. Let xi,jx_{i,j} and yi,jy_{i,j} be the grayscale ground truth pixel values for views AA and BB respectively, sampled over the pixels in the patch. The grayscale values are obtained by taking the average of the RGB channels and multiplying by the mask channel. The patch forms a plane with normal 𝐧\mathbf{n}, placed at depth dd along the ray originating from pixel (u,v)(u,v).

(53) xi,j=ℐA​(u+i,v+j)−2≤i,j≤2\displaystyle x_{i,j}=\mathcal{I}_{A}(u+i,v+j)\qquad-2\leq i,j\leq 2
(54) d′=d​𝐧T​𝐊A−1​(u,v,1)T𝐧T​𝐊A−1​(u+i,v+j,1)T\displaystyle d^{\prime}=d\frac{\mathbf{n}^{T}\mathbf{K}_{A}^{-1}(u,v,1)^{T}}{\mathbf{n}^{T}\mathbf{K}_{A}^{-1}(u+i,v+j,1)^{T}}
(55) yi,j=ℐB​(πB​(πA−1​(u+i,v+j,d′)))\displaystyle y_{i,j}=\mathcal{I}_{B}(\pi_{B}(\pi_{A}^{-1}(u+i,v+j,d^{\prime})))

In the case of xi,jx_{i,j}, we can directly sample the pixels at their centers, whereas yi,jy_{i,j} requires sampling image ℐB\mathcal{I}_{B} with bilinear interpolation so that yi,jy_{i,j} is a continuous function of the plane normal and depth. The sampling coordinates for yi,jy_{i,j} are obtained by intersecting the plane with the neighboring rays, which gives an intersection depth d′d^{\prime}, then back-projecting to 3D space and finally projecting into view B. The ZNCC z∈[−1,1]z\in[-1,1] is then computed by evaluating the first- and second-order moments of the pixel samples, weighted with a Gaussian kernel.

(56) W=∑wi,j\displaystyle W=\sum w_{i,j}
(57) x¯=1W​∑xi,j​wi,j\displaystyle\overline{x}=\frac{1}{W}\sum x_{i,j}w_{i,j}
(58) y¯=1W​∑yi,j​wi,j\displaystyle\overline{y}=\frac{1}{W}\sum y_{i,j}w_{i,j}
(59) x2¯=1W​∑xi,j2​wi,j\displaystyle\overline{x^{2}}=\frac{1}{W}\sum x_{i,j}^{2}w_{i,j}
(60) y2¯=1W​∑yi,j2​wi,j\displaystyle\overline{y^{2}}=\frac{1}{W}\sum y_{i,j}^{2}w_{i,j}
(61) x​y¯=1W​∑xi,j​yi,j​wi,j\displaystyle\overline{xy}=\frac{1}{W}\sum x_{i,j}y_{i,j}w_{i,j}
(62) ZNCC=x​y¯−x¯⋅y¯x2¯−x¯2+ϵ⋅y2¯−y¯2+ϵ\displaystyle\text{ZNCC}=\frac{\overline{xy}-\overline{x}\cdot\overline{y}}{\sqrt{\overline{x^{2}}-\overline{x}^{2}+\epsilon}\cdot\sqrt{\overline{y^{2}}-\overline{y}^{2}+\epsilon}}

We take ϵ=1.0​E−4\epsilon=1.0E{-4} for numerical stability. The Gaussian kernel is separable (wi,j=wi​wjw_{i,j}=w_{i}w_{j}), with the five weights taken from the 7th row of Pascal’s triangle (1,6,15,20,15,6,1)(1,6,15,20,15,6,1), where the first and last bins are omitted since they contribute very little.

I.3. Nonplanar ZNCC

Assuming that the surface is locally planar tends to erase fine geometric details so we propose to remove the planar assumption in the ZNCC computation. Doing so is simple, we just use the actual depth of the neighboring pixels in view A, instead of taking the depth of the ray/plane intersection. This amounts to replacing equation 54 by d′=𝒟A​(u+i,v+j)d^{\prime}=\mathcal{D}_{A}(u+i,v+j). In practice, we actually use a separate implementation to take advantage of the fact that the pixel values yi,jy_{i,j} can be shared with neighboring pixels in view A, which is not the case in the planar case due to adjacent pixels having different plane orientations.

We evaluate mutual visibility over each pixel in view A in a similar manner to the planar case. First, by computing the normal as before and checking its angle with respect to both viewpoints, and second, by applying the same cycle consistency check. Invalid pixels or pixels for which the mutual visibility tests fail are skipped in the computation of the moments in equations 56-61.

I.4. Loss

Our multi-view loss is ℒMV=(1−ZNCC)\mathcal{L}_{\text{MV}}=(1-\text{ZNCC}), summed over all valid pixels in view A. We use the planar ZNCC computation for most of the training since it is more stable, but switch to the nonplanar ZNCC near the end to recover finer details. Note that the grayscale ground truth images and depth maps follow the same coarse-to-fine training regime as the color losses, which means that the small 5×55\times 5 receptive field will actually cover a larger proportion of the field of view in the beginning.

I.5. Backward Pass

The ZNCC computation performs the forward and backward passes in the same CUDA kernel for efficiency. It takes as input the depth maps 𝒟A\mathcal{D}_{A} and 𝒟B\mathcal{D}_{B}, the grayscale images ℐA\mathcal{I}_{A} and ℐB\mathcal{I}_{B} and intrinsic and extrinsic parameters of both cameras. It produces the loss value ℒM​V\mathcal{L}_{MV} along with depth gradients for view A (∂ℒM​V/∂𝒟A\partial\mathcal{L}_{MV}/\partial\mathcal{D}_{A}). The depth gradients are further propagated to the SDF values during the backward pass of the volume rendering.

J.3. Delaunay Triangulation

Assuming points in general position, we prove here that if a tetrahedron is not a Delaunay tetrahedron, then each of its four corners must have a Voronoi neighbor (not necessarily the same) inside its circumsphere.

By contraposition, this will show that a tetrahedron for which any of its four vertices has no Voronoi neighbors inside of the circumsphere must be a Delaunay tetrahedron.

Proof: Assume the tetrahedron IJKL is not a Delaunay tetrahedron. Without loss of generality, we look at corner I. The circumsphere of IJKL contains at least one site strictly inside of it by definition. Let C be the center of the circumsphere and P the offending site: ‖C−P‖<r=‖C−I‖||C-P||<r=||C-I||, with rr the radius of the circumsphere. In other words, C is closer to P than to I, implying that C is not inside the cell of I by definition of a Voronoi cell.

Because C is outside of I’s cell, there must be a site Q, Voronoi neighbor of I, that defines a bisector plane such that C is on the wrong side:

(92) (C−I)⋅(Q−I)>12​‖Q−I‖22\displaystyle(C-I)\cdot(Q-I)>\frac{1}{2}||Q-I||_{2}^{2}

All that remains to show is that Q must be inside the circumsphere of the tetrahedron:

(93) ‖Q−C‖2\displaystyle||Q-C||^{2} =‖Q−I+I−C‖2\displaystyle=||Q-I+I-C||^{2}
(94) =‖Q−I‖2+2​(Q−I)⋅(I−C)+‖I−C‖2\displaystyle=||Q-I||^{2}+2(Q-I)\cdot(I-C)+||I-C||^{2}
(95) =‖Q−I‖2−2​(Q−I)⋅(C−I)⏟>‖Q−I‖22+‖I−C‖2\displaystyle=||Q-I||^{2}-\underbrace{2(Q-I)\cdot(C-I)}_{>||Q-I||_{2}^{2}}+||I-C||^{2}
(96) <‖I−C‖2=r2\displaystyle<||I-C||^{2}=r^{2}

We have shown that II has a Voronoi neighbor QQ inside the circumsphere, which concludes the proof.
